The first Evil Within was a nail bitter and tense. Not exactly scary (say like the first Resident Evil or even Resident Evil 2), but still a fun yet challenging game with elements of stealth as well as combat and resource management.

The Evil Within 2 takes that same formula and notches it up where stealth definitely plays a bigger part, including the abilities to make your stealth kills more lethal and effective. I love the ability to do a surprise stealth kill from around the corner when a Lost is coming upon you. It works, even if they have noticed you but not exactly sure where you are. Plus another great ability to learn is starting the stealth kill from farther behind the enemy so you don't have to close in right next to them.

The story is also a lot easier to follow for me than the first game and for me, feels a lot more engaging. I'm invested and curious to see how things end up in this game. Things seem more straight forward, but there is still a lot of twists and turns in the story plot-line. I'm into Chapter 11 and things have definitely turned themselves into a different direction than I initially thought, but I'm still guessing at a lot of what I think might happen.

Overall, this game definitely seems to take a lot from the Naughty Dog game, The Last Of Us (Part 1). The way the stealth is almost required, and how it works, along with other game-play elements (finding items, crafting, etc) really seems to remind me of that game's mechanics as well as how the story unfolds. I feel so much more invested in this story than I did in the first Evil Within and I love it.

Gone is the black-bar widescreen format of the first game, although I believe it's still a setting you can turn on here, but default is full screen. I actually do play the first game the way it was originally released. Gives a much more claustrophobic feeling for me and increases the tension.

Game-play feels smoother, with responsive controls using a controller. However, when it came to the shooting gallery, I switched to mouse and keyboard in order to get the highest score and gain all the rewards as I found the controller for me was too difficult. But I'm sure if I had the patience, I could have stuck with the controller in that area and still won all the rewards. However, I wanted to get back to the story and the game itself as it's been an addicting wild ride.

Definitely worth it if you liked the first one. At least, that's how I feel. It definitely starts to answer even more questions from the first game as well as the DLC in that game (Kidman's expansion story from the first game). It's all making sense as to what was going on. At least where I'm at in the story.

UPDATE: Just finished the game last night and all I can say, wow! What a story! Powerful, moving, emotional ending! Loved every minute of this game. I dare say I love the story a lot more than the first one, but they do tie together and questions from the first game are answered, but there are still other unanswered ones as well. But overall, an excellent sequel to an excellent first game.

I decided to write this review a bit early for those on the fence here on the day of release, but I plan to write a more proper review later once I've finished the game. So I've played this game for 9 & a half hours at this point, and barely just finished Chapter 4 (of 15+ chapters). First hour and a half was taking it slow and exploring around in the first two chapters, the next six & a half hours was Chapter 3 and doing EVERYTHING you could in the open world level, 30-45 minutes was committed to me doing the special shooting gallery minigames added to the Save Area once you reach Chapter 4 and getting all the rewards, and then the last 45-60 minutes was going through Chapter 4.

I should mention I'm playing on Nightmare difficulty, and playing with almost all my HUD off. Only things I kept on were my reticle, item pick-up info, and some stuff for later like partner health gauge. The game started off REALLY challenging on Nightmare, I was getting my ass handed to me during all of Chapter 2 and the start of Chapter 3, but I really got a handle of it. I managed to kill every single enemy in Chapter 3, mostly with stealth. Learned a few techniques. I explored every inch of Chapter 3, there is a LOT hidden in it. The side-quests are the obvious ones, but they've literally littered the town with so many interesting things off the beaten path. I'll get back to this.

There is so much I want to say, but I don't really know where to start. Firstly, as a horror enthusiast, this is a REALLY neat horror game. On paper and at first it seems pretty basic, but it slowly reveals it has a lot more up its sleeve. I want to say so much, but I also feel I shouldn't to keep most of it a surprise for others who decide to dig into it. All I'll say is if you don't explore Chapter 3 you're doing yourself a huge disservice, there's literally so many fun, interesting, and unique scenarios to find, and not even just in the side-quests. There's also 5 hidden levels of sorts which are worth finding and experiencing in my opinion among everything, and some do some neat things and touches in the game, like there's this ghost woman who if you do her side-quest will begin to haunt you through the whole game, but will not haunt you if you don't do the side-quest..

To be honest I wasn't really sure what to think of it all at first. Chapter 1 & 2 for a example while I was playing I wasn't quite sure what I thought of it, though in retrospective there was a lot of really cool moments, one of my favorites being when you look down a dark corridor with your flashlight and a giant strange black and white fuzzy eye is staring back at you, then blinks and disappears. The game has so many creative touches if you look around and interact with things. And I began to love it more and more as I played Chapter 3, at the start still uncertain but as I began to get into the groove of it I began to love it.

You can tell the team behind this are very passionate for horror and horror games and had a lot of fun making this, it's full of so many small touches everywhere, it's got so much love for other horror stuff. Chapter 2 is in many ways almost like some pseudo walking sim horror game like Layers of Fear is what it reminded me most of, then Chapter 3 experiments with all sorts of things all over the map, and Chapter 4 has some fun with a unique take on defenseless first-person horror, but with reasoning that makes more sense than usual. But things are paced well to not only keep you on your toes but keep things interesting, and feed well into each other so far.

Chapter 3 I think some people will have a gut reaction to dislike the open world chapter it is on principle and initial impressions, and to be honest I wasn't sure what to think at first myself, but it is incredibly unique and begins to become very immersive, interesting, and fun to explore as you go through it. It's NOT an empty open world by any means, literally every area is intentionally designed with no randomized features, and it's better for it. It's basically a giant horror amusement part with surprises tucked away into every corner, if you'll look for them, and a lot of twists and turns as you dig deeper into the overworld and a lot of interesting, fun, and tense scenarios packs into every area of the map almost.

Despite the fact I've played this game for nearly 10 hours now, I'm still fairly early in. There's a lot more I want to say but kind of also just want to discuss, and then plan to play a lot more tomorrow. I'm finding now that I'm done playing for now I can't stop thinking about this game. I feel like this game is a very different beast than the first game, I'm not sure everyone who loved the first game will love this one even and some people who didn't really like the first game may end up loving this (it still is tellable it's The Evil Within and made by the same team, but they have made some very bold decisions and tried some very different things design wise which kind of makes The Evil Within all at once reminds of several things, and yet feel rather unique on its own, kind of like the original game but in a completely different way).I can already tell this game is going to go on at the very least to become a cult classic with some sectors of horror fans, it's surprisingly unique in many ways and if you let it, it can really begin growing on you.

The Evil Within 2 is a horror gaming gem that takes the genre to new heights. The game skillfully weaves a compelling narrative with intense gameplay, immersing players in a nightmarish world. Sebastian Castellanos’ personal journey adds emotional depth, while the open-world design enhances exploration.

Visually striking and eerie, the game’s environments and creatures deliver a potent dose of horror. Improved controls make for a smoother experience, and the balance between action and tension is finely tuned. The result is a sequel that not only meets but exceeds expectations, offering a thrilling and chilling adventure for horror enthusiasts. The Evil Within 2 is a must-play for those seeking a gripping and atmospheric gaming experience.

The first Evil Within was, when all is said and done, a mish-mash of just about every "survival horror" cliche under the sun. The game had no compunctions, whatsoever, about proudly flying the influence of every major horror game released since the early Resident Evils and Silent Hills...all the way up to the latest-and-greatest released in the twenty-odd years since, such as Outlast and The Last of Us.

   It got away with such brazen plagiarism for one reason and one reason alone: it was good. Real good. Probably as good as the best games which helped spawn it, and better than all the rest. Anyone who enjoyed that first instalment should be pleased to hear that not that much has changed for the sophomore outing.

   I mean, sure, no one should be surprised to hear that everything's a wee bit "bigger" this time around. More action, more gore, more stealth, more weapons, more crafting, more "open world"-ish elements, and two - count 'em, TWO - different types of safe/save rooms. We all expected this. The good news is that they haven't gone ape-shit with any of it, and the basic charms of the original game remain intact. It's much the same thing, with just a few more mechanics and options, and an ever-so-slightly darker (and, arguably, superior) storyline. 

   Heck, I was happy. Extremely happy. As I'm sure most fans of the first will be. Clearly one of the best horror games of the year, in a very, VERY good year for such things.

Verdict: 10/10.

(PS Don't believe this game, kids: coffee isn't actually good for your health. Though come to think of it, neither is pretty much anything else portrayed in the game. As you were.)

(PPS I generally hate "side-missions". I really do. This game has some of the most worthwhile side-missions ever, which not only reward the player with the expected "goodies", but with some genuinely interesting side-plots, backstory, and/or just-plain-creepy ideas. That said, I hope Bethesda don't go getting any grander ideas for Evil Within 3, 'cause I'm really not that interested in playing the horror equivalent of Borderlands...)

Video Games are usually surreal and a bit ridiculous, that’s a big part of why I love them. The Evil Within 2 really embodies these characteristics and alot more good stuff too. 

I mean it is definitely a sequel with Sebastian Castellanos back in action, kicking ass again!
However some aspects of the game are very different in tone and structure from the first one.

I completed the first game just before starting this one and it is surreal how different this one is while also paying plenty of tribute to it's predecessor. The Evil Within 2 is kinda disjointed but in an interesting way as it all feels atmospheric and well thought out.

There are linear sequences that are really similar to the gameplay of the first game but also open world sections which feel completely different to play. The overall tone is also less creepy than the first game while instead being more surreal and campy.

There is some excellent fan service and nods to the first game that are implemented in fun ways. While the writing is bad in a funny way (which I think is intentional) while also being really good and well structured in some parts. 

Some of Castellanos’ dialogue in this game is hilarious and totally awesome. The first game did have a sense of humour too but the sequel takes this aspect even further. As he says some of the most ridiculous and badass things throughout the campaign.

I laughed a lot at comments such as ‘tell that to my brain’ or hearing him yell ‘fuck that!’ as he runs away from a pack of zombies. While I was also genuinely impressed by how they added depth to his character with a compelling backstory.

The open world sections are well designed and fun to explore while the weapons are also really satisfying to use. They distribute the weapons and ammunition in a clever way that influenced my sense of vulnerability and power at just the right moments. 

Like in the beginning you feel vulnerable and everybody you meet is talking about trying to find weapons. Then when you actually get a good one it feels really satisfying to start kicking some ass, especially with the shotgun….. BOOM! BOOM!

This sequel is both well designed and lovingly put together as an enjoyable game in it’s own right and also as a tribute to the first Evil Within. I will be keeping an eye out for a third entry in the series to complete Sebastian Castellanos’ badass trilogy of ass kicking!!!

10/10 – A Masterpiece of Emotion, Storytelling, and Heart

The Evil Within 2 isn't just a horror game—it's an emotional journey that completely took me by surprise. I went in expecting some creepy monsters and jump scares, but what I got was so much deeper: a story full of love, guilt, friendship, and sacrifice that left a lasting impression on me long after the credits rolled.

I found myself genuinely connecting with almost every character. The relationships felt real, the emotions were raw, and the pacing was just perfect. There were moments of hope, despair, fear, and even warmth that I honestly didn’t expect from a survival horror title. It pulled me in so hard that I would forget to do my work because I was so invested in seeing what happened next.

Yes, the zombie AI was kind of dumb at times, and there were a few glitches here and there (some were even kind of funny), but honestly? I didn’t care. The combat wasn’t the highlight for me anyway. It was the story—and oh my god, what a story. The ending left me both heartbroken and satisfied. Some characters… I just didn’t want to say goodbye to, but it is what it is.

This game has its hiccups, but they don’t matter when everything else is this good. The narrative alone is strong enough to carry the entire experience. If you’re looking for a game that delivers more than just scares—something that hits your heart as much as your nerves—The Evil Within 2 is it.

The Evil Within 2 is a third person survival horror game where the player once again controls the main character from the previous game, Sebastian Castellanos, who must return to the virtual world of STEM, in search of his daughter Lily.

The good
•	Gameplay is what I expect from a survival horror game. You’ll fight against a small number of enemies who are all legitimately dangerous (which is different from action games that typically throw large numbers of weak enemies at you). Ammo and health supplies are limited, so careful resource management is vital.
•	You can find several weapons including a knife, fire axe, pistol, shotgun, crossbow (which can fire five different types of bolt), assault rifle, sniper rifle, and a flamethrower.
•	Use stealth to sneak up behind enemies and perform an instant melee kill.
•	Some of the action takes place in a small town, which provides a more open level design. This allows you the possibility of avoiding some enemies to conserve ammo. You’re also encouraged to explore the environment and search for supplies. Components can be crafted into ammo and health items at a workbench, whilst weapon parts can be used to upgrade the damage, clip size, rate of fire and reload speed of your weapons.
•	Green gel gathered from fallen enemies can be spent to upgrade your health and stamina, and to acquire special abilities such as a chance to dodge attacks, or survive hits that would normally have killed you.
•	Visual design of the monsters is quite unique.
•	The personal story involving Sebastian and his family is fairly interesting, and the motivations of the villains are well written. They’re not just evil for the sake of being evil [spoiler] although the photographer is basically a copy of Sander Cohen from Bioshock[/spoiler].
•	Voice acting is mostly good.
•	The first game had several enemies and traps that could instantly kill the player, which I found quite frustrating. I can only recall this happening to me once during the sequel.
•	It took me 16.5 hours to finish the story and I didn’t suffer from any crashes.
•	Controls are mostly rebindable and work well with mouse and keyboard.

The bad
•	Although I was able to easily maintain a solid 60 fps, I suffered from a frequent stuttering effect. There are countless reports of this problem on the forum, but unfortunately no definitive fix. Lowering graphics settings doesn’t seem to help. It doesn’t make the game unplayable, but it does at least partially spoil the experience.

The recommendation

The Evil Within 2 is definitely worth playing if you’re a fan of survival horror games, but I would suggest waiting for a further optimisation patch, or a sale. You might also want to consider playing the first game to get the background of the story and characters.

The Evil Within 2 presents us with a more solid gameplay experience and an open world that includes side missions, but it comes at a cost.

The game shifts from survival horror to action survival experience, with a little touch of horror. The bosses in the first game, like Laura and The Keeper, are more memorable compared to this one.

The dialogues are corny and the storytelling execution is good, but could be better.

As previously mentioned, The Evil Within 2 provides a better experience than its predecessor in terms of gameplay. The open world is well-suited to the game, though sometimes the combat can become repetitive.

If you're looking for a tense and authentic horror experience with a creepy atmosphere like the first game, maybe you'll be let down. However, The Evil Within 2 can provide a delightful survival-action experience.

The Evil Within 1 and 2 were the games that introduced me to horror games (same with Outlast & Outlast: Whistleblower, but The Evil Within took it a step further with incredibly intelligent writing, an awesome semi-open world and a well fleshed-out combat system). Therefore I share one of my earliest and best gaming experiences with this franchise. If you loved The Evil Within 1, you will definitely love this one too. There really couldn't have been a better and more emotional sequel than this.

[i]The Evil Within 2[/i] introduces a lot of changes. Sebastian, who was once a hardboiled detective, a man of few words, now suddenly talks a lot and expresses his feelings. A malicious person might call him a whiner, but despite that, he remains a tough cowboy who is also a caring father. The sequel adds more depth to the characters that was lacking in the first game, but it is less creative with character/environment designs and the level of craziness, opting for a more urban sci-fi direction rather than leaning into gritty horror. The game is definitely more comfortable to play, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the gameplay is better. The first [i]The Evil Within[/i] is much harder and has a deeper combat system.

The story is straightforward and conventional, filled with plenty of expositional dialogue. It strives for optimism, family, love, and logic—everything must be explained, which is often typical of American storytelling (the director and screenwriter are Americans this time). "Everything will be alright" is the story this game tells. Some will enjoy it, while others will look for more mystery, darkness, ambiguity, and philosophizing (the kind of narration often found in Asian and European media). It really depends on personal preference.

That being said, the ending is very sweet and touching. No matter how different they are in their storytelling, I highly recommend both games, and I hope that one day there will be a third. It would be silly to drag Sebastian into everything again—other characters have the potential to become new protagonists and antagonists. I’m looking at you, Joseph Oda.

Long story short: Sebastian Castlevania 2: Electric Boogaloo. It's the sequel I needed, but not the sequel I wanted.

The Evil Within 2 is a survival horror game. Unlike it's predecessor, it's also semi-open-world and adds a gather-and-craft mechanic. As you explore this small town, you must shoot or sneak your way through, solve really simple puzzles and upgrade your skills. Now with Weapon Parts, weapon upgrades are now separated from Green Goo cost, which allows steady progression for both skills and weapon upgrades. With the last update, you can also change the game into First Person View which can spice things up.

Stem... A bizarre machine created by Ruben "Ruvik" Victoriano whose purpose is to connect multiple minds together into 1 single "core" person. Inside this dream world, anything is possible but the core must be stable or else, all hell can break loose... 3 years after the events of TEW1, Sebastian Castellanos is now a washed-up ex-cop who likes to take naps on bar tables. Out of nowhere, he gets a second chance of finding his daughter Lily but she's held captive by Mobius, the company who wanted Stem from Ruvik back in TEW1. Now Mobius have their own Stem system but Lily is lost in it. Sebastian, being a Stem veteran foot soldier is then sent inside this highly unstable dream construct to clean up the mess.

On the graphical side, TEW2 is a step up from TEW1. Character models and facial animation are amazing, just like TEW1. Textures and model depth feels nex-gen, something TEW1's DX9 engine couldn't pull off with its "plastic toy" look. The small town sections in the first part of the game might feel a bit boring like any suburb, however it does get better as you progress. Cutscenes are well-tailored and camera works gives it an action movie edge.

In the sound department, again, voice actors are the main stars. The story is delivered in a dramatic and heartfelt way, and so does Sebastian's voice actor as well as the supporting characters. However, they could have reduced the amount of times Seb says "What the...?", but I guess this is a sort of funny one-liner now. The music is also noteworthy, mostly during cutscenes.

Now, let's dive in the [i]nightmarish[/i] side of this dream world.

What makes a great sequel is usually following up to what the first game set up to do but in a better way. If the gameplay formula is changed, it should be slightly, here and there, without putting aside the previous installment core ideas. After playing TEW1 for +120 hours and getting 70/71 achievements, it's clear my mind was set on what TEW in general was about. But then I stepped in TEW2 and felt really alienated, both in story and gameplay.

It's not how the story is told, it's the odd direction it has taken. The main antagonist from TEW1 is completely ignored and instead the story focuses on the DLC's antagonist, Mobius. Seb isn't looking for Leslie/Ruvik, he's looking for Mobius. But then his dead daughter is suddenly alive, held by Mobius, inside Stem? Can I have a truckload of cheesecake and peeled onions please?

On the gameplay side, this game favors stealth above all. Your fancy pistol aiming skills from TEW1 won't matter as enemies bob their head all over the place, so consecutive headshots are difficult to pull off. Enemies will often gank you if you don't stealth. They all run and attack very fast. It's easy to get overwhelmed if you don't run back fast enough. So in this game, it's mostly about how much ammo you can hoard until you fail a stealth kill and spend your ammo on the imminent gank squad. But you run far enough in a bush and it's like nobody saw you, Sneak 100 Skyrim-style.

In TEW1, weapons had a better chemistry with how enemies reacted to them, since stealth wasn't such a big deal. Each situations required intelligent use of each guns and applying your gun tactics felt satisfying. Conserving ammo was crucial because you couldn't craft it. The Matchstick mechanic is completely gone. You can't burn dormant enemies anymore. You can't burn a corpse while a live enemy is standing above. Corpse firebombs where a thing in TEW1, oh yes. Why take that away?

Meanwhile in TEW2, conserving ammo is a chore because stealth is the ultimate ammo saver. Crossbow with electric arrow is found at the start, which makes crowd control easy. Crossbow requires less gunpowder in general, so it's easy to cheese arrow crafting and crowd-control more. Why spend 2 shotgun shells and 12 pistol rounds on these 3-4 enemies? Just run around, gather them, shoot an upgraded electric arrow and stomp them one by one. Or you know, stealth kill them and keep your arrow...

The way Tango changed the game formula reflects on how poorly the first TEW was received. Instead of sticking to their guns, they bended over and tried to appeal to the mass. It's so obvious because as a whole, TEW2 feels more like a TEW spinoff title than an actual sequel. I fear Bethesda might have forced Tango's hand on this one, sadly...

The Evil Within 2: An Emotional and Atmospheric Masterpiece
Overall Rating: Highly Recommended

I absolutely love the "semi-open world" approach of this game. Being able to explore the environment at my own pace, rather than being forced down a strictly linear path, makes the experience much more immersive.

An Emotional Journey
The story of The Evil Within 2 is nothing short of amazing. The ending was so deeply moving that I was nearly brought to tears. Seeing Juli Kidman back in action was a highlight for me as well. She feels like a perfect blend of Jill Valentine and Ada Wong—a truly badass female protagonist who commands every scene she’s in.

Technical Performance: Laptop vs. Desktop
I had to complete my first playthrough on my gaming laptop, which is significantly less powerful than my main rig at home. Because I work in a different city during the week, I only have access to my high-end PC on weekends.

On my laptop, I had to play on the lowest graphical settings, which was far from ideal. Even then, the frame rate was unstable and rarely hit 60 FPS. I also experienced two crashes during my run, though I suspect my hardware was to blame rather than the game itself, as I haven't seen many streamers encounter similar issues. I am looking forward to starting New Game Plus on my superior PC to finally see the game in its full glory.

Gameplay and Horror
Survival Horror: The horror elements are very well-executed. Ammo is limited, forcing you to make strategic decisions about when to stand your ground and when to run.

Enemy AI: The AI is surprisingly clever. For example, the "Harbinger" (the flamethrower enemy) can only be sneak-attacked once before he becomes highly alert, making it almost impossible to catch him off guard again.

Monster Design: The creatures are incredibly creepy and challenging. I also enjoyed the nostalgic tension of facing off against bosses from the first game.

Final Thoughts & DLC Hopes
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed the game. I am really hoping for a Kidman-centered DLC, similar to the first game. I’d love to see what she was doing while Sebastian was inside STEM or what happened immediately before they met at the bar. Additionally, I’m curious about Joseph’s fate and would love to see his story expanded upon in future content.

If you enjoy survival horror with a heart-wrenching story, this is a must-play. Thumbs up!

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 241:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ (10/10)

[i]The Evil Within 2[/i] is one of the most underrated horror games out there, and I'll die on that hill. You can still feel Shinji Mikami's influence, but the sequel does a great job of finding its own identity. It mixes survival horror, action, exploration, and just enough freedom to make the whole thing click. One minute you're carefully sneaking past some grotesque nightmare, the next you're frantically running for your life because you made the mistake of looking at something you really shouldn't have. It's creepy, it's tense, it's fun, and it knows when to move things along. Honestly, this is survival horror done right.

[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Combat. The guns feel powerful, aiming is responsive, and headshots actually matter. Ammo is limited enough that you have to think about whether it's worth fighting an enemy at all. Maybe you take the shot, maybe you sneak around it, or maybe you set a trap and let it do the work for you. Stealth is also useful, though it doesn't make you feel completely safe.

[*] The upgrade and crafting systems are satisfying. Green gel is back, and it feels great to put it toward upgrades for your weapons, health, stamina, and stealth. You can really feel Sebastian getting stronger, and deciding what to prioritize matters. Crafting is great, too. You can make supplies out in the field if you're desperate, but it costs more, so you're always deciding whether to risk it or wait until you're back at a workbench. It's a simple system, but it works really well.

[*] The semi-open world is a fantastic addition. Union is divided into sections that give you room to explore without bloating the game. You can approach objectives in different ways, investigate optional locations, follow side stories, or wander into some creepy house because you spotted something interesting. And of course, you might regret going inside. Exploration feels worthwhile because you're weighing the potential rewards against the risk of running into something horrible. 

[*] The horror is creative as hell. The environments are constantly changing, from blood-soaked galleries to warped school hallways and sterile laboratories that somehow feel even more unsettling than the bloody ones. The game blends psychological horror, body horror, and outright nightmare fuel.

[*] You actually care about the story. Sebastian Castellanos may have been a generic cop in the first game, but in[i] Evil Within 2,[/i] he’s a grieving father on a desperate rescue mission. That motivation makes the whole journey feel more personal. He's still dealing with his own trauma and demons, both literal and figurative, but there's a real emotional core underneath all the horror. 
[/list]
 [b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] A couple of late-game enemies feel like bullet sponges. By the final chapters, the game shifts more into action-horror and throws tougher enemies and bosses at you. While it’s not a huge deal, some of the encounters can feel more tedious than tense, especially if you didn’t upgrade the right gear. But that’s minor compared to how strong the rest of the game is.

[*] Can be pretty slow-paced. Lots of sneaking, waiting, backtracking, etc. To me, this adds to the atmosphere, but it can be frustrating for other players.
[/list]

Unfortunately, I am a bit puzzled with the 8/10 and 9/10 reviews for this... As a fan of the first game, this is mostly a lot different experience. My first problem is with the voice acting - as ALL of the voice actors have been replaced (not sure why?). In the end, I got used to Sebastian´s more expressive lines and acting but Kidman sounds so vulnerable, nothing like a cold hearted focused woman she was in the first one, her voice just not fits this time. Tatyana´s is not far off but she lost that exotic feel in her voice and sounds more generic, but still decent. 

Story is much more straightforward and clear - get in, grab your daughter, get out. Things get complicated as you can expect but there are not too many surprises. One of the biggest downsides is that main villain (quite interesting one) gets at some point replaced with a generic guy which I thought was a mistake... The ending is also easy to comprehend and however, even though they were trying to pull emotions out of me, I still felt nothing. I just could not care about any of the characters in the game much, which is a shame. I was a bit angry and confused at the end of TEW due to lack of explanation, but here there was nothing, it just ended and I did not feel the need to play this game again.

Gameplay has been completely revamped - you are thrown into semi-open world and while I was scared at first I won´t like it, I must admit it is done well and I had fun doing all the objectives in chapter 3. Then you begin a proper hunt for the killer in STEM world - the claustrophobic rooms return while you are on his trail and you are surrounded with lots of creepy stuff. However, after two open areas, you [spoiler]finally catch the killer and are given new objective, new "crazy priest kind of guy" to hunt down, which I felt was forced into the game to make it longer.[/spoiler] The other half of the game is simply not interesting nor engaging enough - areas are just gray corridors which repeat or levels you have been in just with a different sky texture and extra enemies. What spices up the gameplay this time instead of pre-scripted Ruvik sequences, is Anima - a new deadly foe, which insta kills you if she sees you. This definitely add extra layer of fear as she can randomly spawn almost anywhere and when you see cold mist manifest and hear her singing, you have to run and hide. 

Developers also changed engines so a lot of the feel and look of the game is different from one. While the characters look more detailed, I would not say they look necessarily better, just different and I still like the original in this regard. Sound effects, I think, are a lot worse and sound more amateuristic. While the enemy sounds in first game were terrifying and unsettling, these just sound like something from a B movie, very cheese and not authentic.

Overall, while not a bad game, TEW2 just can´t pull off the same vibe and atmosphere as TEW. It has a different direction and I appreciate it tried to do something new with semi the open world areas, however, it falls short in repetition in the later levels and lackluster, emotionless story (I felt they tried to play the daughter card too hard). I´d recommend this getting on a sale, not at full price. I hope there will be TEW3, maybe with Mikami back at the helm and more interesting story and gameplay blend of larger and smaller areas.

This is another one of those games which are good if we look at them by themselves, and... moot if we compare them to the earlier game. 
This is the issue with Steam's recommendation system: would I recommend it? Yeah. Do I think this game deserves a bit of backlash for the direction it took after the first game? Absolutely, and I'll explain more about it later. But Steam will just turn all of that into a statistic based on whether people recommend the game or not.

So.
The Evil Within 2 is a cool, fun horror game.

But I'm going straight to the point: it is very far from being as scary and mysterious as the first game was.

It's a lot more action-oriented, stealth is busted, and some parts take place in semi-open-world areas.

Should I explain that a horror game where you can run into large open areas, where the moment you step into a bush the enemies lose you and you can stab them, is way, way, WAY less scary than a game where you walk through narrow, claustrophobic corridors, with nowhere to hide and very little ammo?

It's not just "less scary", it's "not scary."

And I find that a bit ironic considering that The Evil Within 1 was made by some former Resident Evil developers who thought the games had become too action-oriented and wanted to make their own game and go back to real horror. And they did it with the first game. It was truly horrific.

Now, you're absolutely not scared. In fact, I didn't feel like the prey in this game; I felt like the predator. I felt like most of the enemies were just trapped in here with me, not the other way around.

That's actually what happens in the story in a way, because here, Sebastian Castellanos willingly goes into the STEM when he learns that his daughter might still be alive in there and that he could save her.

The character completely changed from the first game. He went from a depressed, broody cop who had lost everything and was fighting for his life, to Liam Neeson in Taken, who's coming after the bad guys to save his daughter. It felt way more like a generic Hollywood action movie.

Just so you understand my point better: I almost didn't use any bullets in this game, because you can almost always use stealth to stab enemies. In the first game, you were stressed because ammo was scarce and you actually NEEDED it. Here, you don't even need your weapons most of the time.

So... why am I still recommending it?

Like I said, it's a good game on its own. I liked it.

And to be honest, I'm not gonna complain that I was able to relax while playing this game instead of constantly clenching my buttocks.

And even though the more linear aspect of the first game worked in its favor when it came to the horror, it was still painfully linear. The gameplay of the second game is really more fun, and it's refreshing to have way more freedom.

It's just that it's a shame that they decided to give up the horror identity that was the spearhead of this new franchise and go for more action-oriented gameplay and Hollywood-style writing, where the hero is just a badass guy who wants to kick ass, chew gum, and save his goddamn family!

You can even feel it in the art direction. Sebastian is literally unrecognizable from the first game; his features are more bland. His clothes are more bland too. The first game had some kind of classic detective outfit, with a noir aesthetic that they completely threw away. Honestly, it felt a bit like a middle finger to the first game.

This game gave me a lot of mixed feelings, so I'll try to list everything.

Cons:

- I don't like the new voice actors. Overall, as the game goes on, you kinda stop caring, but for example Sebastian's voice actor can only really pull off those suffering, miserable tones, and I buy those. But whenever he starts yelling or uses pretty much any other emotion - not at all (imho).

- The visual style changed. In the first game there was this oppressive, rusty vibe, and I praised it because even the game's age wasn't that noticeable thanks to it. Here they completely changed direction. The game is still pretty dark, but it feels flat and empty somehow. The graphics got upgraded, but they can't really save it because the visual identity took a hit.

- Why are the dialogues so damn cringe? It has the same kind of feel as other Bethesda games. The camera locks into place, dialogue choices are presented in the same way, character gestures often don't match what's being said, and everyone's faces are practically made of stone. A very weird decision.

- A minor complaint since it's just an optional setting, but the game clearly wasn't designed around first-person mode. I decided to play that way at first, but dropped the idea pretty quickly. It's awkward and looks kinda janky. That's probably why there are only one or two first-person segments in the entire game.

- Story + bosses. I liked the story less than in the first game. The plot here is completely predictable (wow, a father tries to save his family, loses his companions, gets haunted by the ghosts of his past) and there's way less psychological mindfuckery going on. Even the bosses are fewer in number, which also hurts the overall vibe and visual identity. There are fewer bosses, and they're worse quality-wise. Most of them are basically people who mutated into some kind of zombies, while in the first game they were genuinely twisted, corrupted creatures and people (and not just people, by the way) that only a sick imagination could come up with. Father Theodor only shows up and gets revealed as the bad guy after you're already past the halfway point of the game. That said, credit where it's due: the boss designs in the second game are actually pretty cool.

Pros:

+ Open world. The idea of having a small open-world area across several chapters is pretty neat, especially since the location can change in the next chapter. There are lots of side activities scattered around: side missions, resources, files, keys, and so on. Personally, I think the game could've stayed fully linear without losing much of that content. I'd probably prefer that approach, but I still liked what they did here.

+ The flashbacks to the first game were done really well, and the boss rush featuring guys from the first game was awesome.

+ OST and sound design. They're okay for most of the game, but toward the end, in the final chapters, they become genuinely pretty good.

+ Chapter 17 is really cool, but it suffers from the same issues as the rest of the game (vibe, predictability, etc.).

+ Gameplay. It is almost the same as in the first game. The only real additions are the mostly useless cover system and some tweaks to the upgrade system (it honestly feels like changes for the sake of changes — nothing fundamentally new or significantly different was added). But that's not really a major downside. The core gameplay formula is still just as enjoyable and solid as before.


Conclusion:

The Evil Within 2 is a genuinely good game. I can completely understand people who consider it a 10/10. It's great that the game gives them that many positive emotions. I got those emotions too, just not as strongly as I did from the first game.

If you look at it as a standalone game, it's solid and easily deserves an 8.5/10. But compared to the first game, it feels like a small step sideways, and in some aspects even a downgrade, so I'd rate it a 7.5/10.

Considering we're probably never getting another sequel, I'll settle on an 8/10.

Evil Within 2 therefore surprised me with how well balanced it actually is. Watching IGN's review of the game made me initially thought this was some difficult AF survival game where you're always running low on resources. But that isn't true. The game wasn't as hard as I thought. Resources are aplenty given the non-linear scope, and most enemy encounters can be cheesed away with stealth kills. Still, the game puts itself together with a wonderful format of both a mix of open world levels and linear levels. The game does however re-use the same levels multiple times, which seems pretty lazy to me, but even the same levels don't remain the same when you return to it. The nature of STEM also allows for fun horror elements to play out you'll only find in your wildest dreams and rapid changes in the environmental variety as you can find yourself in something like a jungle then in a icy landscape the next chapter. 

The horror aspect is another rather well-done part and I loved the unique boss fights here, an aspect that seems only doable by the Japanese for some reason... (do western devs have no creativity or something?). But the game splits itself a little all over the place with more than one villain. Without spoiling too much, after the first half of the game or so, the horror aspect wears off quite quickly as the level themes changes to reflect the new villains that pop up. I also find it funny Sebastian can battle all the enemies merely by using bullets but whatever, it's a Resident Evil thing I suppose.

Apart from these complaints, the game is really solid irregard-less. Combat is fun. Stealth, while a bit too easy most times, never really gets tiring thanks to the brilliant kill animations. And the story is one long but satisfying journey to the end as Sebastian fights tooth and nail to get his daughter back no matter what.


Pros:
- Great open level design mixed with non-linear parts along the way
- Horror is uniquely great... at the beginning up till first half...
- Combat is fun and well balanced
- Decent single player length
- Satisfying closure to Sebastian's story (I hope, pls let the poor guy have peace already)

Cons:
- Stealth can make most enemy encounters way too easy
- The scare factor kinda wears off after the first half of the game when the intrigue disappears
- Story is a little all over the place with multiple villains and the mid-portion feels a bit tacked on

Overall score - 8/10

Evil Within 2 is the essence of B-Movies and J-Horror mixed together with all the skill and subtlety of an industrial blender. 

That is to say, this game is very, [b]very[/b] dumb. The plot makes literally no sense other than to ferry you along from horror showcase to horror showcase, yet despite that, there's something weirdly compelling about it. You know the plot is garbage, but it's still interesting garbage. 

The game itself is a kind of horror-survival over-the-shoulder thing; EW2 doesn't particularly do anything new, but if you've ever played Resident Evil 4, you'll kind of know the drill. Some of the weapons are even pretty fun to use, like the big ol' crossbow you get early on. The combat's actually kind of fun, and you're still underpowered enough that you can't just blindly rush in most of the time, especially on the higher difficulties. 

And to reiterate, do not think about the plot of this game too hard. Enjoy the game for what it is; a fun romp through cheesy horrorland, not a masterful psychological horror. This game is fun in the way a haunted carnival ride is fun, and if you go in with this attitude, the game will reward you accordingly.

Konami and Capcom are carelessly walking down a hall, each from opposite ways. Suddenly they collide: 
"Hey, you got your Silent Hill in my Resident Evil!"
"Well you got your Resident Evil in my Silent Hill!" 
Bethesda, watching from a distance:
"That gives me an idea..."

Seriously though, I've had The Evil Within 2 sitting in my library for ages, and I recently decided to play it without any expectations other than it's a psychological horror game made by a decent developer. What I didn't expect was just how good of a Silent Hill/Resident Evil mashup this game would be. The game provides both an entertaining third person shooter experience and a chilling psychological trip. 
Even down to the enemy designs, you have mindless zombies rushing at you one moment, and the next you have an amalgamation of flesh and metal hunting you down, moaning in disturbing pleasure at the thought of ripping you a new one.

I never actually played The Evil Within, I did however watch a playthrough of it, so I knew the story. But I believe that TEW2 is a better experience than the first, mainly due to the open-ish world environment. You can explore the crumbling town of Union at your own pace, spending as little or as much time as you like finding hidden items and supplies, which I recommend you do if you play on Nightmare difficulty. 

And I highly recommend you do play on Nightmare, the stronger enemies and worryingly low supply of ammo will leave you fighting for your life until the very end of the game. There's nothing I hate more than having maxed out ammo at the end of a survival game; it deflates all the tension. Rest assured, in Nightmare mode you will be counting your lucky stars if you have a full clip. You will have to rely on keen resource management and exploration to get through it, which I believe is the very essence of any survival horror worth its salt.

The game is fairly long for a single player narrative game, however it feels a little artificially inflated at some points. You get to a section you might think is the climax, only to discover it's the ending of the second act, and that you still have plenty of game to chew through. Not to say that the whole experience wasn't enjoyable, it just didn't feel like it was all planned out from the very beginning. 

The combat is engaging, especially in Nightmare mode. Enemies feel threatening throughout the game, and killing them is thoroughly satisfying. However the stealth sections do reveal that their AI is pitiful. They have the memory of a goldfish, regularly forgetting I existed if I duck behind a wall. And their tunnel vision allows me to sneak up behind them fairly easily to go in for the backstab kill. 

All in all, The Evil Within 2 was a deeply enjoyable game that I did not see coming. Its price is still inexplicably steep despite it being years old at this point. I would suggest picking it up on sale, and you will have a great time.

TL;DR This survival horror feels like Silent Hill and Resident Evil combined, and is a welcome addition to Bethesda's impressive selection of quality games.
